title: Election Day storm could impact voter turnout in key midterm states | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

A soggy storm will track through the central United States on Election Day and could influence voter turnout forkey races in the region.

Confidence is growing for widespread rain from parts of the Great Lakes and Upper Midwest to the western Gulf Coast Tuesday, but exactly who gets the most disruptive soaking is still in question.

We’ll know more by this weekend, but for now, it’s looking like parts of Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Texas, and maybe even Ohio, could contend with wet conditions.

Gusty winds could also accompany the rain in the Midwest and Plains. Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain are possible threats on the storm’s southern side from Texas to the lower-Mississippi Valley.

The conditions will be a turnout factor in those states and for others in the central US who aren’t among the more than39 million people who have already cast ballotsthrough early voting.

Rainfall and other active weather tend to suppress voter turnout while sunshine has the opposite effect,multiplestudieshavefound.

Dry weather will likely bookend the storm along much of the East Coast and in the West. The only exception is coastal areas of the Southeast where nuisance showers can’t be completely ruled out yet.

There will be no need to bundle up. High temperatures in most of the nation’s eastern half are forecast to be 5 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit above average. Only the Southwest will have temperatures tilting a bit cooler than average.

The breakdown below shows the forecast for some of the key states in the midterms. Keep in mind these forecasts will likely change as confidence grows in the storm’s path by this weekend.
